segments.narration: Nine hikers cut their tent open from inside. February 1959, the northern Urals. They ran out into minus thirty wearing almost nothing.
Searchers found them scattered down the slope. Two lay by a dead fire under a cedar, their hands burned from climbing it.
The injuries made it worse. Crushed ribs. A fractured skull. And almost no marks on the skin above them.
The file was sealed for decades, so the theories grew instead: secret weapons tests, infrasound, even a yeti.
In 2020 Russian prosecutors reopened it and named a slab avalanche. A year later physicists modelled the slope doing exactly that.

research.summary: The 1959 Dyatlov Pass incident: nine ski-hikers died on Kholat Syakhl in the northern Urals after cutting their way out of their tent at night. Russia reopened the case in 2019 and concluded in 2020 that a slab avalanche was the cause; a 2021 paper in Communications Earth & Environment modelled how the shallow slope could produce one.

segments.narration: There is a book no one on Earth can read. Two hundred and forty pages of tidy handwriting in a script that matches nothing.
Radiocarbon dating puts the vellum in the early fourteen hundreds, so it is not a Victorian forgery on old skin.
The drawings do not help. Bathing women in green pools, spiral star charts, and plants that match no living species.
Codebreakers who cracked wartime ciphers took it on and lost. Every announced solution has collapsed under review.
Statisticians say the text behaves like a real language, with word patterns a hoaxer would struggle to fake by hand.

research.summary: The Voynich manuscript is an illustrated codex written in an unknown script, radiocarbon dated to the early 15th century and held at Yale's Beinecke Library as MS 408. Its plants are largely unidentifiable and no proposed decipherment has been accepted.

segments.narration: A telescope heard something once and never again. August 1977, Ohio. Seventy-two seconds of narrow radio noise from Sagittarius.
Jerry Ehman found it on the printout days later. He circled the letters and wrote one word in the margin: Wow.
It sat almost exactly on the hydrogen line, 1420 megahertz. That frequency is protected, and it is where you would listen for someone.
Seventy-two seconds is exactly how long the beam took to sweep that patch of sky, so the source was out there, not on Earth.
Dozens of searches since have found nothing there. A 2017 comet explanation was proposed, and other astronomers took it apart.

research.summary: The Wow! signal was a 72-second narrowband radio burst detected by the Big Ear telescope on 15 August 1977, near the 1420 MHz hydrogen line, from the direction of Sagittarius. Jerry Ehman circled the printout and wrote 'Wow!'. It has never been redetected.

The inquiry blamed a freak wave catching all three during a storm. Islands like that throw water higher than anyone expects.

segments.narration: Australia declared war on birds and lost. November 1932, Western Australia, and the enemy was twenty thousand emus.
The birds were flattening wheat that soldier-settlers had been given after the First World War. The farmers asked for machine guns.
They got them. Two Lewis guns, ten thousand rounds, and a major to run the operation.
Emus do not stand still. They split into small groups, ran at fifty kilometres an hour, and absorbed hits that should have dropped them.
The final count was under a thousand birds for nearly ten thousand rounds. The operation was quietly dropped and fences were built instead.

research.summary: The Great Emu War of late 1932: after 20,000 emus moved into Western Australian wheat farms, the Minister for Defence sent soldiers with Lewis guns. The operation was withdrawn in November, resumed, and ended in December with roughly 986 birds killed from 9,860 rounds.

segments.narration: A flower bulb once cost more than a house. Amsterdam, sixteen thirty-seven, and the flower was a tulip.
The prized bulbs were streaked with flame patterns. Nobody knew why, and nobody could reliably breed them.
Buyers traded contracts in taverns for bulbs still in the ground, months from flowering. Nobody was holding a tulip.
In February the buyers simply stopped turning up at an auction in Haarlem. Prices fell to nothing within weeks.
The cause was mundane: a virus made the streaks, and the crash hit a small circle of traders. The Dutch economy barely noticed.

research.summary: Tulip mania in the Dutch Republic peaked in the winter of 1636-37, when contracts for rare tulip bulbs reached extraordinary prices before collapsing in February 1637. Modern historians, notably Anne Goldgar, have shown the crash's wider economic damage was far smaller than the legend claims.

segments.narration: Hunter-gatherers built a stone temple before farming existed. Southeastern Turkey, around nine thousand five hundred BC.
The pillars are T-shaped limestone, up to five and a half metres tall, weighing as much as ten tonnes each.
They are covered in carved animals. Foxes, scorpions, vultures, boars. Not hunting scenes. Something closer to a cast list.

Five women sued in nineteen twenty-seven and settled. Their cases forced the law to recognise disease caused by work, and shaped US safety standards.

segments.narration: A man sent 4000 deliveries to a stranger for a bet. London, twenty-seventh of November, eighteen ten.
The target was a Mrs Tottenham, who had done nothing at all. The prankster was a writer named Theodore Hook.
It started with chimney sweeps at dawn. Then coal wagons. Then wedding cakes, doctors, lawyers, and a hearse with coffins.
Hook had rented a room straight across the road so he could sit and watch it happen all day.
By evening the street was solid. The wager was reportedly a guinea, and Hook simply left London for a while until it blew over.

He carried two letters and could manage a handful of phrases. He could write one thing clearly: his own name.
He told them he had grown up alone in a dark cell, fed bread and water by a man he never saw.
Europe became obsessed. One theory made him a hidden prince of Baden, swapped as a baby to steal a succession.
In eighteen thirty-three he staggered home with a stab wound and died three days later. DNA tests since have been contradictory, and the case is still open.

segments.narration: A wave of beer killed eight people in London. Seventeenth of October, eighteen fourteen, in the St Giles rookery.
A seven-metre fermentation vat gave way. Its iron hoop had failed hours earlier and had been reported as nothing to worry about.
When it went, it took the other vats with it. More than half a million litres of porter hit the street at once.
St Giles was one of the poorest districts in the city, and families lived in basements. The beer poured straight down into them.
Eight people died, all women and children. The inquest called it an act of God, the brewery paid nothing, and it later got its excise duty refunded.

Eight people died. An inquest ruled the deaths an act of God and no compensation was paid.

segments.narration: Two scientists dynamited fossils to spite each other. Eighteen seventies America, and they were the founders of dinosaur science.
Edward Cope and Othniel Marsh started as friends. Then Marsh publicly pointed out that Cope had put a plesiosaur's head on its tail.
After that they raced. Bribing each other's crews, intercepting shipments, and rushing descriptions into print to claim a name first.
Crews were told to smash what they could not carry, so the other man's team would find nothing worth digging.
They named a huge share of the dinosaurs a child can recognise today, including Triceratops and Stegosaurus, and both died broke and disgraced.

research.summary: The Bone Wars were a rivalry between palaeontologists Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel Charles Marsh from the 1870s to the 1890s. Between them they named well over a hundred new dinosaur species, while using bribery, spies and site destruction. Both men ended their careers financially and reputationally damaged.
